# Data

You will be working with a subset of human rights textual data originating from the PULSAR project, maintained by the Text(Co)Lab at the University of Pittsburgh. The datasets contain web-scraped news feeds, blog posts, expert notes, interviews, and other news-like texts published by organizations working on human rights violations and protection. You will work with data from three organizations: (1) Anti-Slavery International; (2) the Center for Victims of Torture; and (3) Save the Children.

The dataset contains the following variables:

- `source`: the organization that published the text (Anti-Slavery International, Center for Victims of Torture, or Save the Children)
- `country`: the country the text refers to
- `date`: the publication date of the text
- `text`: the full text of the document
- `slavery`: whether the text is about slavery (1) or not (0), as coded by a human annotator

For more information, see: Text(Co)Lab. (2020). *PULSAR - Data* (Version 2) [Data set]. Harvard Dataverse. https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/0MEMHG
Link: https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataset.xhtml?persistentId=doi:10.7910/DVN/0MEMHG


# Exercise 1. Data Pre-Processing and Data Visualization 

### Questions

**Question 1.** First, if feasible, get to know your texts. Read the text entries and try to spot weird'' and noisy’’ elements (e.g., URLs, emails, emojis, boilerplate text, and editorial notes). In short, look for anything that adds unnecessary detail and does not relate to human rights. Once you have done that, pre-process your corpus of human rights news-like texts using the cleaning techniques you have seen in class that are appropriate given the nature and peculiarities of the data. Explain all the pre-processing steps you applied and argue why you applied them. Write your R code below and explain EVERY SINGLE LINE with a comment (#) in your own words *(max. 400 words)*

**Answer** Before starting the text analysis, I first looked at the dataset and at some original articles from each organization to see what kind of information they contained. I noticed that the texts included not only article content, but also website code, links, email addresses and contact details. These elements were not relevant to our analysis, so I decided to remove them.

First, I converted all the text to lowercase. This is important because words written with capital and small letters should be treated as the same word. I then removed HTML scripts and comments, as they sometimes contained technical website information rather than actual article content.

Next, I removed URLs, website links and email addresses. I also removed editorial notes and contact information, such as the interview details that appeared at the end of some articles. I did this because I wanted to focus on the actual content of the articles, rather than information about the websites or the organizations.

After that, I replaced punctuation with spaces and removed numbers. This follows the preprocessing steps discussed in class and makes the texts more consistent for word analysis. Finally, I replaced multiple spaces and line breaks with a single space and removed unnecessary spaces at the beginning and end of each text.

I put all these steps into a Clean_Text() function and applied it to the entire dataset. I saved the cleaned articles in a new column called clean_text, so that the original texts remained available for comparison.

To check whether the cleaning worked, I compared the original and cleaned versions of the articles and checked for missing values. The results showed that all 910 articles had been cleaned successfully, with no missing values.

One limitation is that removing all numbers also means losing potentially useful information, such as years and statistics. However, I kept this step because it was part of the preprocessing method taught in class.

*Hint*: If you find something peculiar in the texts and are unsure how to remove it with regular expressions, ask a GenAI tool for help. If you do, report what it suggested and whether the suggestion was useful.  *(max. 200 words)*

**Answer**

I used ChatGPT to help identify how to remove some unusual elements found in the original articles. In particular, one Anti-Slavery International article contained HTML comments with JavaScript code, while some Save the Children articles included contact information at the end, such as telephone numbers and email addresses.

I asked ChatGPT how to remove these elements using regular expressions in R. It suggested using gsub() to remove HTML comments and scripts, and a separate regular expression to remove the contact section starting with “For interviews or more information please contact:”.

The suggestions were useful because they helped me adapt the cleaning function to the specific content of my dataset. I tested the code by comparing the original and cleaned texts. and the HTML code and contact information were successfully removed.

```{r}

head(df) # display the first six rows of the dataset

glimpse(df) # check the column names and data types

examples <- df %>% group_by(source) %>% slice_head(n = 1) %>% ungroup() # Select one text from each organization

for (i in 1:nrow(examples)) {  cat("\n\nORGANIZATION:", examples$source[i], "\n"); cat(examples$text[i], "\n") } # print the original texts to unnecessary information

Clean_Text <- function(text){ # text cleaning
  temp <- tolower(text) # convert everything to lowercase
  temp <- gsub("(?s)<script[^>]*>.*?</script>", "", temp, perl = TRUE) # remove HTML script elements
  temp <- gsub("(?s)<!--.*?-->", "", temp, perl = TRUE) # remove HTML comments, which can contain website code
  temp <- gsub("(s?)(f|ht)tp(s?)://\\S+\\b", "", temp) # remove URLs
  temp <- gsub("www[.]\\S+", "", temp) # remove links that start with www.
  temp <- gsub("\\S+@\\S+", "", temp) # remove email addresses
  temp <- gsub("\\b[a-z]+[.][a-z]{2,3}/[a-z0-9]+\\b", "", temp) # remove short URLs
  temp <- gsub("(for )?(any )?queries with respect to.{0,150}?editor", "", temp, perl = TRUE) # remove editorial notes mentioning queries and contacting the editor
  temp <- gsub("(?s)for interviews or more information please contact:.*$", "", temp, perl = TRUE) # remove contact-information footers
  temp <- gsub("[[:punct:]]+", " ", temp) # replace punctuation with a space
  temp <- gsub("[[:digit:]]+", "", temp) # remove numbers
  temp <- gsub("[[:space:]]+", " ", temp) # replace repeated spaces, tabs and line breaks with one space
  temp <- trimws(temp)} # remove spaces

df$clean_text <- Clean_Text(df$text) # apply the cleaning function to the whole dataset

## comparing the original and cleaned texts

substr(df$text[1], 1, 500) # display the first 500 characters of the original article

substr(df$clean_text[1], 1, 500) # display the first 500 characters of the cleaned article

head(df$clean_text) # display the first six cleaned articles

sum(is.na(df$clean_text)) # count how many articles have missing cleaned text

length(df$text) # check the number of original articles
length(df$clean_text) # check the number of cleaned articles

```

**Question 2.** Next, conduct a frequency analysis of unigrams, bigrams and trigrams in your pre-processed corpus. For each, report the most frequent terms (e.g., the top 20). Then comment on the results: Which terms and collocations dominate the corpus? Do they relate to human rights issues or do you still see noise that your pre-processing missed? What do bigrams and trigrams reveal that unigrams do not? Do the most frequent n-grams differ across the three organizations? Write your R code below and explain EVERY SINGLE LINE with a comment (#) in your own words. *(max. 500 words)*

**Answer** 

For the unigrams, the most frequent words are “children” (4,206), “slavery” (2,586), “cvt” (2,086), “people” (1,889), “work” (1,749) and “torture” (1,593). Most of these terms are directly related to the topics covered by the organizations. However, some words, such as “cvt”, “anti” and “save”, mainly refer to the organizations themselves. Other words, such as “one”, “also” and “said”, are quite general and do not tell us much about the actual topics.

When looking at the bigrams, we get a clearer picture of the issues discussed. The most frequent combinations are “save children” (958), “anti slavery” (938), “human rights” (843), “slavery international” (584) and “forced labour” (410). Other interesting combinations include “modern slavery”, “child labour”, “human trafficking” and “mental health”. These expressions give us more information than individual words because they show which concepts are discussed together.

The trigrams provide even more detail. The most frequent one is “anti slavery international” (573), followed by “population refugees migration” (81), “bureau population refugees” (80) and “center victims torture” (68). We also find relevant expressions such as “modern slavery act”, “human rights violations” and “mental health care”. However, some trigrams mainly refer to organization names or institutional information rather than human-rights issues.

When comparing the three organizations, we can see that their most frequent terms are quite different. Anti-Slavery International mainly discusses slavery, forced labour, trafficking and domestic workers. CVT focuses more on torture, survivors, refugees and mental health. Save the Children mainly discusses children, families, education, humanitarian aid and child protection.

In general, the results show that most of the frequent terms are relevant to the organizations' work. However, some noise remains, including organization names and administrative expressions such as “please contact”. This suggests that the preprocessing removed much of the unnecessary information, but not everything. The use of bigrams and trigrams helps us identify more specific topics and understand the context in which individual words appear.

```{r}

corpus_hr <- corpus(df, text_field = "clean_text") # create a corpus with the cleaned texts

summary(corpus_hr) # check the corpus

tokens_hr <- tokens(corpus_hr) # create tokens from the corpus so each article into individual words

tokens_clean <- tokens_select(tokens_hr, pattern = stopwords("en"), selection = "remove", min_nchar = 2) # remove English stopwords and words with fewer than two characters that are not informative

## UNIGRAMS

dfm_uni <- dfm(tokens_clean) # create a document-feature matrix containing individual words

topfeatures(dfm_uni, 20) # display the 20 most frequent individual words in the corpus

## BIGRAMS

tokens_bi <- tokens_ngrams(tokens_clean, n = 2) # combine consecutive words into pairs

dfm_bi <- dfm(tokens_bi) # create a document-feature matrix containing bigrams

topfeatures(dfm_bi, 20) # display the 20 most frequent bigrams in the corpus

# TRIGRAMS

tokens_tri <- tokens_ngrams(tokens_clean, n = 3) # combine consecutive words into groups of three

dfm_tri <- dfm(tokens_tri) # create a document-feature matrix containing trigrams

topfeatures(dfm_tri, 20) # display the 20 most frequent trigrams in the corpus

dfm_uni_source <- dfm_group(dfm_uni, groups = docvars(dfm_uni, "source")) # group the unigram document-feature matrix by organization

lapply(seq_len(ndoc(dfm_uni_source)), function(i) {topfeatures(dfm_uni_source[i, ], 20)}) # display the 20 most frequent unigrams for each organization

dfm_bi_source <- dfm_group(dfm_bi, groups = docvars(dfm_bi, "source")) # group the bigram document-feature matrix by organization

lapply(seq_len(ndoc(dfm_bi_source)), function(i) {topfeatures(dfm_bi_source[i, ], 20)}) # display the 20 most frequent bigrams for each organization

dfm_tri_source <- dfm_group(dfm_tri, groups = docvars(dfm_tri, "source")) # group the trigram document-feature matrix by organization

lapply(seq_len(ndoc(dfm_tri_source)), function(i) {topfeatures(dfm_tri_source[i, ], 20)}) # display the 20 most frequent trigrams for each organization

```

**Answer** 

The unigram word cloud shows that “children” is the most frequent term, followed by words such as “slavery”, “people”, “work”, “torture” and “international”. This reflects the main topics covered in the articles. The bigram cloud provides more specific expressions, with “human rights”, “save children”, “anti slavery”, “forced labour” and “mental health” appearing prominently. The trigram cloud gives further detail by highlighting phrases such as “anti slavery international”, “population refugees migration”, “center victims torture” and “modern slavery act”. Overall, the three word clouds show that the dataset focuses on children’s rights, modern slavery, human rights violations and support for vulnerable groups. While the unigram cloud gives a broad overview, the bigrams and trigrams reveal more specific themes and organisations mentioned in the articles.

```{r}

dfm_uni %>% # use the unigram document-feature matrix containing all articles
  textstat_frequency(n = 15) %>% # create a table of the 15 most frequent words
```

# Exercise 2. Sentiment Analysis

**Question 1.** Run a sentiment analysis of the corpus using the Lexicoder Sentiment Dictionary, which comes with quanteda. Explore the results in the way you find most insightful (e.g., distributions, plots, comparisons across organizations or over time). Then reflect on the method: Is it appropriate? And does it make sense to run a dictionary-based sentiment analysis on this kind of data? Why or why not? Argue. Write your R code below and explain EVERY SINGLE LINE with a comment (#) *(max. 500 words)*

```{r}

# create a dictionary with positive and negative words

sentimentdict <- dictionary(list(pos = data_dictionary_LSD2015$positive, # Select the positive words from the Lexicoder dictionary
  neg = data_dictionary_LSD2015$negative  # Select the negative words from the Lexicoder dictionary
))

# calculate sentiment for every article

sentiment_hr <- df %>% # use the human rights articles
  corpus(text_field = "clean_text") %>% # create a corpus using the cleaned text
  tokens() %>% # split each article into individual words
  dfm() %>% # count every word in each article
  dfm_lookup(sentimentdict) %>% # count positive and negative dictionary words
  convert(to = "data.frame") %>% # convert the results into a regular data frame
  mutate(sent = pos - neg) # calculate sentiment as positive words minus negative words

sentiment_hr$n_words <- ntoken(tokens(corpus(df, text_field = "clean_text"))) # Count the words in each article

sentiment_hr$sent_per_100 <- sentiment_hr$sent / sentiment_hr$n_words * 100 # Standardise sentiment scores by article length

sentiment_hr <- cbind(df[, c("source", "date")], sentiment_hr[, -1]) # Combine article information with sentiment scores

summary(sentiment_hr$sent_per_100) # Show the main statistics of the sentiment scores

## visualisation

ggplot(sentiment_hr, aes(x = sent_per_100)) + # put sentiment scores on the x-axis
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue") + # show the distribution using 30 bars
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") + # add a dashed line for neutral sentiment
  labs(title = "Sentiment Distribution Across Human Rights Articles", # add a plot title
       x = "Sentiment per 100 words", # label the x-axis
       y = "Number of articles") + # label the y-axis
  theme_minimal() # apply a clean plot theme

## compare organisations

ggplot(sentiment_hr, aes(x = source, y = sent_per_100, fill = source)) + # compare sentiment scores by organisation
  geom_boxplot() + # show the distribution and median for each organisation
  labs(title = "Sentiment by Organisation", # add a plot title
       x = "Organisation", # label the x-axis
       y = "Sentiment per 100 words") + # label the y-axis
  theme_minimal() + # apply a clean plot theme
  theme(legend.position = "none") # remove the unnecessary legend

```

**Answer** 

The sentiment is slightly negative, with a mean score of -0.53 and a median of -0.75 per 100 words, This suggests that negative words appear somewhat more frequently than positive words across the corpus. There are also some differences between the organisations. However, this does not necessarily mean that the articles themselves have a negative message. CVT Blog has a positive median sentiment, while Anti-Slavery International and Save the Children have negative medians. This could be related to the topics they cover and the way they communicate. For example, articles discussing torture, abuse, forced labour or human trafficking will naturally contain many words that the dictionary classifies as negative. 

The method using the Lexicoder Sentiment Dictionary is useful to get a first overview of the sentiment in the articles, but as the dictionary simply counts positive and negative words without really understanding their context, the interpretation of the analysis needs to be done carefully. Thus, I believe the method is not sufficient on its own for this type of data.

**Question 2.** Run a sentiment analysis of the corpus using NRC Word-Emotion Association Lexicon. Explore the results in the way you find most insightful (e.g., distributions, plots, comparisons across organizations or over time). Then reflect on the method: Is it appropriate? And does it make sense to run a dictionary-based sentiment analysis on this kind of data? Why or why not? Argue. Write your R code below and explain EVERY SINGLE LINE with a comment (#) *(max. 500 words)*

```{r}

nrc_scores <- get_nrc_sentiment(df$text) # count emotions in every article

n_words <- ntoken(tokens(corpus(df, text_field = "text"))) # count the total number of words in each article

nrc_hr <- cbind(source = df$source, n_words = n_words, nrc_scores) # add the article information to the emotion scores

nrc_long <- nrc_hr %>% # use the NRC results
  pivot_longer( # convert the emotion columns into two columns
    cols = -c(source, n_words), # keep the organisation and word count unchanged
    names_to = "emotion", # store the emotion names in a column called emotion
    values_to = "count" # store the emotion counts in a column called count
  )

nrc_long <- nrc_long %>% # use the NRC table
  mutate(score_per_100 = count / n_words * 100) # standardise the emotion counts by article length

nrc_summary <- nrc_long %>% # use the NRC results
  group_by(source, emotion) %>% # create groups for each organisation and emotion
  summarise(mean_score = mean(score_per_100), .groups = "drop") # calculate the average emotion score per 100 words

nrc_summary # display the average emotion scores for each organisation

## Visualisation

ggplot(nrc_summary, aes(x = reorder(emotion, mean_score), y = mean_score, fill = emotion)) + # put emotions on the x-axis and their average scores on the y-axis
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) + # draw one bar for each emotion
  coord_flip() + # flip the axes to make the emotion names easier to read
  facet_wrap(~ source) + # create a separate plot for each organisation
  labs(title = "NRC Emotion Distribution by Organisation", # add a plot title
       x = "Emotion", # label the x-axis
       y = "Average count per 100 words") + # label the y-axis
  theme_minimal() # use the minimal plot theme

```

**Answer**

The NRC dictionary gives us a more detailed picture of the emotions expressed in the articles, as it identifies eight emotions in addition to positive and negative words. Looking at the results, positive words are the most frequent across all three organisations, followed by negative words. Trust is also quite prominent, while surprise and disgust appear less frequently.

There are some differences between the organisations. Anti-Slavery International has relatively high counts of both positive and negative words. CVT Blog stands out for its higher level of trust, while Save the Children has higher scores for fear and sadness. This could be related to the different topics they focus on and the way they communicate.

However, we need to be careful when interpreting these results. The dictionary simply identifies words associated with certain emotions, without really understanding the context in which they are used. For example, an article about torture or child abuse may contain many words associated with fear or sadness, even if the purpose of the article is to raise awareness or call for action.

I think the NRC dictionary is useful to explore the emotional content of the articles and identify some differences between organisations. However, it does not fully capture the meaning or intention behind the texts. Human rights articles often deal with serious and sensitive issues, so dictionary-based sentiment analysis should be seen as a starting point rather than a definitive measure of the emotions expressed.

**Question 3.** In your own words, explain the difference between the Lexicoder Sentiment Dictionary and the NRC Word-Emotion Association Lexicon. Then name three text data settings in which running a sentiment analysis makes sense, and explain why. *(max. 500 words)*

**Answer**

The main difference between the two dictionaries is what they measure. The Lexicoder Sentiment Dictionary focuses on positive and negative words, giving us a general idea of whether a text is more positive or negative. The NRC Word-Emotion Association Lexicon goes a bit further, as it also identifies eight emotions: anger, anticipation, disgust, fear, joy, sadness, surprise and trust. So, while Lexicoder gives us an overall sentiment score, NRC allows us to look in more detail at the emotions expressed in the text.
Sentiment analysis can be useful in many different situations. For example, companies can use it to analyse customer reviews and get an idea of what people think about their products or services, including what customers like and what could be improved. It can also be used to look at reactions on social media, for instance, to see how people respond to a particular event, campaign or political decision. Another example is news articles, where researchers can examine how certain topics or public figures are presented in the media and whether the language used is generally more positive or negative. Sentiment analysis is useful for identifying general patterns in large amounts of text, but dictionaries do not really understand the context in which words are used, thus, the results need to be interpreted carefully, as they do not always reflect what the texts actually mean or what the author is trying to communicate.

# Exercise 4. Supervised ML: Predicting if a text about slavery or not

*Question 1.* Using the human-coded slavery variable as your outcome, train at least two supervised machine learning classifiers (e.g., Naive Bayes and a logistic regression/a random forest) to predict whether a text is about slavery. Split your data into a training set and a test set. Write your R code below and explain EVERY SINGLE LINE with a comment (#) in your own words.

```{r}
df$slavery <- factor(df$slavery, levels = c(0, 1)) #convert outcome into 0/1 factor

set.seed(123) #set seed to control randomness


data_split <- initial_split( #initiate a split of the data
  df, #from df object
  prop = 0.80, #with a proportion of 80% for the train set; 20% for the test set
  strata = slavery) #strata ensures the resample have equivalent proportions as the original data set

train <- training(data_split) # store the training observations in a unique data frame
test <- testing(data_split) #store the testing observations in a unique data frame


train_dfm <- corpus(train, text_field = "clean_text") %>% #create a dfm from cleaned train set text
  tokens(remove_punct = TRUE, remove_numbers = TRUE) %>% #remove punctuation and digits
  tokens_remove(stopwords("en")) %>% #remove stopwords
  dfm() %>% #
  dfm_trim(min_docfreq = 5, docfreq_type = "count") #set up frequency and type

test_dfm <- corpus(test, text_field = "clean_text") %>% #create a dfm from cleaned test set text
  tokens(remove_punct = TRUE, remove_numbers = TRUE) %>% #remove punctuation and digits
  tokens_remove(stopwords("en")) %>% #remove stopwords
  dfm() #

# Make the test matrix contain the same word features as the training matrix.
test_dfm <- dfm_match(test_dfm, features = featnames(train_dfm)) # Match the test set of a dfm to a train set of dfm)

nb_model <- textmodel_nb( #train Naive Bayes classifier
  train_dfm, #with dfm from train text
  y = train$slavery, #from slavery column
  distribution = "multinomial", #set the distribution
  smooth = 1 #to do 
)

nb_pred <- predict(nb_model, newdata = test_dfm) #predict category of test set with Naive Bayes

x_train <- as(train_dfm, "dgCMatrix") #convert train dfm into matrice for glmnet function
x_test <- as(test_dfm, "dgCMatrix") #convert test dfm into matrice for glmnet function

# Train a cross-validated LASSO logistic-regression classifier.
set.seed(123) #control randomness and ensure reproductibility
logit_model <- cv.glmnet( #glmnet fits a generalized linear model via penalized maximum likelihood
  x = x_train, #input matrix
  y = as.numeric(as.character(train$slavery)), #response variable
  family = "binomial", #character string
  alpha = 1, #elasticity parameter
  nfolds = 10 #number of lambda
)

logit_prob <- predict( #probability that a document is actually about slavery
  logit_model, #from previous object logit_model
  newx = x_test, #matrice to use for prediction
  s = "lambda.min", #standard error
  type = "response" #type of outpout prediction
)

logit_pred <- factor( #convert probabilities into factor
  ifelse(logit_prob >= 0.50, 1, 0), #using 0.5 threshold
  levels = c(0, 1) #with a binary response 0/1
)
```

*Question 3.* Which words are most predictive of a text being about slavery? Do they make substantive sense? Interpret. *(max. 500 words)* 

```{r}

```

**Answer**
The logistic regression coefficient shows which words are the most strongly or not to whether the text is attributed to slavery or not. Positive coefficient will predict class 1 (slavery related) or class 0 (not slavery related).

The ten most predictive words about slavery are: "sold", "panel", "pickers", "estimate", "anti", "conviction", "accused", "guilty", "twitter", and "arrested".
Some of them have a clear-cut relation with slavery: "sold", "pickers" are words that refer to human trafficking, exploitation, and forced labor. " Pickers" is a term specifically used for force agricultural labor. Additionally, "conviction", "guilty", or "arrested" may be linked to investigations and legal proceedings in the event of slavery or trafficking.
On the other hand, words such as "anti" or "estimate" or twitter" are not per se related to slavery. "Anti" is most probably linked to Anti Slavery International which constitutes the bulk of the documents (see question 4). Twitter may refer to the social network as a source of information listed in the documents, but it is not related to slavery in itself. Finally, estimate may refer to estimation of whatever traffic but could not be categorized as slavery-related.
Some others top words in the list are also connoted with slavery ("abducted", "recruiting", "combating"). Overall, it appear that the results are well affiliated with the core topic.
